titulo.texto: Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick

frase_gancho.texto: Two enormous hands hold Frida up so she can let go of her crutches.

puente_narrativo.texto: Leave the painting halls behind and continue to the next stop on your route.

guion_corto.texto: In this painting from nineteen fifty-four, Frida appears wearing a corset, her crutches about to fall. Karl Marx, the German philosopher of the nineteenth century, holds her up with his hands. It is a painting of political hope. In those months Frida felt very close to the ideas against injustice, poverty, and racism. She painted it in the last year of her life, while her health was getting worse. The museum keeps it here, in the painting halls. It measures about sixty centimeters wide by seventy-six high. It is small, but it says a great deal about how she wanted to be seen.

guion_largo.texto:
The title is already a statement. Marxism will give health to the sick. Frida painted it in nineteen fifty-four, in the last year of her life. It is an oil on Masonite of about sixty by seventy-six centimeters.

Look first at Frida. She appears wearing a corset, which she really did wear because of her spine. The crutches are about to fall because Karl Marx, the German thinker of the nineteenth century, holds her up with his hands. The museum explains it this way. Marx holds Frida up so that she can let go of her crutches. It is an image of relief, almost of a miracle.

According to the best-known reading of the painting, to one side Marx chokes an eagle that has the head of Uncle Sam. A dove also appears, a symbol of peace. These are very clear symbols, from a time when the world was divided by the Cold War.

To understand the painting, we need to remember Frida's political history. In nineteen twenty-seven she joined the Mexican Communist Party, before marrying Diego Rivera. Trotsky and his wife lived in her home between nineteen thirty-seven and nineteen thirty-nine. In nineteen fifty-four she was still defending her ideas. On July second, barely eleven days before she died, she took part in a protest march in a wheelchair. It was a way of saying, until the very end, which side she was on.

The museum tells us that Frida identified with the ideas against injustice, poverty, violence, and racism. In the painting, that conviction is mixed with something very personal. Her body had been through many operations. She lived with pain. The idea of a force that could heal the sick had a meaning for her that went beyond politics.

Some people compare the composition to that of an ex-voto. In those popular paintings, a saint appears in the sky to save a person. Here the saint is Marx and the person is Frida. We do not know whether she thought of it that way, but the comparison helps us see how she blended popular faith with her ideas.

The political context of those months helps us understand the painting. In June of nineteen fifty-four, the government of President Jacobo Árbenz fell in Guatemala, in a coup backed by the United States. The march of July second, which Frida attended, was a protest over that event. It is likely that those ideas were very much on her mind when she painted this picture.

After looking at the painting, keep one question in mind. Is it a work of propaganda or the dream of a sick person? Surely both.

texto: Look for the two crutches about to fall and the hands that hold Frida up
Find Karl Marx, the eagle with the head of Uncle Sam, and the dove of peace
Notice the corset Frida wears in the painting, the same kind of device you will see later in the dress hall

texto.Title: Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Frida became interested in politics only to follow Diego Rivera.
texto.respuesta: Reality: She joined the Mexican Communist Party in nineteen twenty-seven, before marrying Diego in nineteen twenty-nine, and she remained active until eleven days before she died.
